tools.description: Search every meeting transcript for a phrase. Start here when you do not already know which meeting you want — it returns matching lines with surrounding context instead of whole transcripts. Matching is fuzzy by default, because transcripts are speech recognition output that mangles names and jargon — "evals" arrives as "evalves", "QLoRA" as "cue lura". Fuzzy hits carry match_type and, when the words differ from the query, matched_text — what was actually transcribed — so you can judge each one. Pass match="literal" for exact-phrase search. Each hit carries the meeting id and an utterance_index you can pass to get_transcript as `offset` to read on from that point. Responses are capped by total size, so a page may hold fewer hits than `limit` asked for. When truncated is true there are more hits — truncation_reason says why the page ended — and calling again with cursor=next_cursor gets them.

tools.description: List recorded meetings, newest first. A meeting that is still recording or not yet transcribed is listed with processed=false and no speakers. Most rows carry a summary: a paragraph saying what that meeting was about, so a whole month can be scanned here rather than by reading transcripts. Titles are weak evidence: they come from calendar invites and window titles, and are often wrong, stale, or shared by unrelated meetings — to find a meeting by who was there or what was said, use search_transcripts instead. Each row also carries tags: one Context, at most one Format and at most one Topic, each with origin "human" (a person chose it) or "auto" (chosen on device, and may be wrong).

tools.description: Read one meeting's transcript. Supply either a time window (start_time/end_time, seconds from the start of the recording) or an utterance window (offset/limit) — not both. Use detail="full" to get what the pipeline knows about each line: how confident the speaker attribution was, whether the speech overlapped someone else, whether the speaker was in the room (stream="microphone") or on the call (stream="system"), and where their name came from — label_origin runs human (typed) > voiceprint (biometric) > inferred (heard in the conversation) > generated (placeholder), strongest first. Responses are capped by total size, so a page may hold fewer utterances than `limit` asked for; when truncated is true, truncation_reason says why the page ended, and calling again with offset=next_offset continues.

detail.description: "text" for speaker and words only; "full" to also get confidence, overlap, stream and label origin, plus bleed_suspected — the room was measurably echoing the call during this line, so if it reads oddly, that may be why; a hint, not a verdict — and during_utterance_index, the turn this line occurred entirely inside, which tells speech that interrupted a turn apart from listening noises within it. Default "text". "full" is cheap on a narrow window — pair it with offset/limit to check individual suspect lines.

end_time.description: Window end, seconds from the start of the recording.

include_tokens.description: Include per-word timings and confidences. Large; default false.

meeting_id.description: The meeting's UUID, from list_meetings or search_transcripts.

min_duration_seconds.description: Drop lines shorter than this many seconds — backchannels like 'Yeah.' are typically under ~1.5s. The filtered count comes back as utterances_filtered_out.

start_time.description: Window start, seconds from the start of the recording.

tools.name: get_transcript

tools.description: One meeting's metadata: when it ran, what recorded it, who spoke and for how long, and a quality block saying how much to trust the transcript — per-stream durations, acoustic bleed from the speakers into the microphone, and the share of lines whose speaker attribution was weak. Cluster ids are assigned per stream, so a speaker's identity is the (stream, cluster_id) pair — the same cluster_id on two streams is two people. When the meeting was matched to a calendar event, the invitees (attendee_names, with attendee_kinds saying which of them are people, groups or rooms) and the scheduled slot (scheduled_start, scheduled_end) are returned too — the slot is what the calendar intended, where started_at/ended_at are what happened — and title_origin says whether the title is trustworthy: "calendar" came from the invite, everything else was guessed. A speaker nobody has named may carry suggestions — names heard in the conversation, each with tier ("strong" or "weak") and the quoted line it came from, whose utterance_index you can pass to get_transcript as `offset` to read around it. They are guesses with evidence attached: judge them by the quote. label_origin runs human (typed) > voiceprint (biometric) > inferred (heard in the conversation) > generated (placeholder), strongest first. tags, suggested_tag and tags_stale are as in list_meetings.

tools.description: The corpus as people rather than meetings: who has spoken, in how many meetings, for how long, and when they were first and last heard. People are identified by enrolled_voice_id, the only key that links a speaker across meetings — a speaker with no enrolled voice cannot be linked, and appears as a separate entry per meeting. Such an entry is still findable by name when the conversation supplied one: name_contains matches names heard on tape as well as names on file, and an unenrolled entry carries suggested_name and tier when a name was only guessed at rather than applied. An empty result is still not proof of absence — search_transcripts for the name instead. Each entry lists at most 20 of that person's most recent meetings — meeting_count and total_speaking_seconds always cover all of them — and when truncated is true there are more people: call again with cursor=next_cursor.
